overview: This file brings together State Department material on Japan’s electric-power system and its dependence on imported resources between 1940 and 1943. Its principal document is a March 1941 despatch from American Consul Samuel Sokobin reporting improved power and tram service in Kobe as rainfall, hydroelectric generation, and coal supplies increased, while emphasizing that rapidly growing coal and salt exports from occupied China revealed Japan’s mounting military-economic dependence on Chinese resources and its willingness to disregard shortages in Shanghai and among Chinese civilians. An internal departmental memorandum summarizes that despatch, and a cross-reference sheet points to a February 1940 report on Japanese power shortages. Two later letters document J. R. Thomas’s donation to the Department of a technically detailed 1923 annual report of the Toho Electric Power Company.

subfiles.title: Thomas letter forwarding a 1923 Toho Electric Power Company report
subfiles.about: Thomas offers the State Department a copy of the Toho Electric Power Company’s detailed annual report for possible government or military use.
subfiles.summary: Thomas states that he found the report while reviewing his files and believes its technical information and diagrammatic maps of electrical generation, transmission, and distribution may still be useful. He also calls attention to its legal, financial, and cultural data, despite the report being twenty years old, and suggests that the Department retain it or pass it to the Armed Services.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledgment of the Toho report
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges receipt of Thomas’s letter and the enclosed Toho Electric Power Company report dated April 30, 1923.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks Thomas for supplying the report. He notes that it has been brought to the attention of Department officers directly concerned with Japanese affairs and expresses appreciation for Thomas’s thoughtfulness.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Grew report on Japan’s electric-power shortage
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to a February 1940 report on Japan’s electric-power shortage and its enclosed ministerial notification and newspaper clipping.
subfiles.summary: This filing aid cross-references an original paper filed as 894.50/118. The referenced document, sent from Japan by Grew, reported on the shortage of electric power and enclosed a ministerial notification and a clipping from the Japan Advertiser.

subfiles.title: Departmental memorandum summarizing Kobe despatch no. 115
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes Samuel Sokobin’s report on easing Japanese power restrictions and Japan’s growing dependence on coal imported from China.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum attributes the reported alleviation of Kobe’s power restrictions partly to greater hydroelectric output but primarily to increased coal supplies, with an accompanying rise in sulphate-of-ammonia production. It highlights the absence of Japanese press references to Chinese coal imports while Shanghai experienced shortages. The memorandum emphasizes the extraordinary growth of Chinese coal exports to Japan and the Kwantung Leased Territory as evidence of Japan’s increasing dependence on China and its disregard for both Chinese consumers and Japanese interests in Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Despatch on improved Japanese power production and imports of Chinese coal
subfiles.from: Samuel Sokobin, American Consul at Kobe
subfiles.about: Sokobin reports improved electric-power conditions in Kobe while analyzing Japan’s rapidly increasing extraction of coal and salt from China for industrial and armament needs.
subfiles.summary: Sokobin reports that increased rainfall and coal supplies had eased power restrictions in Kobe, restored municipal tram schedules, and improved sulphate-of-ammonia production. He contrasts Japanese publicity about domestic coal production with the lack of acknowledgment that imports from China had risen from 615,745 metric tons in 1935 to 3,846,368 in 1940, even while Japanese textile mills in Shanghai suffered from power shortages. Customs figures also show large coal shipments to the Kwantung Leased Territory and Korea, with Japan and its territories taking 96.7 percent of China’s 1940 coal exports. Comparable growth in salt exports, together with severe salt scarcity around Hankow, leads Sokobin to characterize Japanese policy as ruthless resource exploitation driven by armament and strategic requirements.

interest: The file is especially useful because it links a localized improvement in Kobe’s electricity and public transport to the much larger political economy of Japan’s wartime expansion. Sokobin’s despatch supplies unusually concrete annual trade statistics and shows how American diplomats interpreted coal and salt movements as indicators of military capacity, imperial exploitation, and strategic dependence on China. The 1943 correspondence adds a separate intelligence-history dimension by showing the State Department collecting a two-decade-old corporate engineering report for possible wartime use.
